The biggest issue with automation is that it can't all be done at once, and it can't all be synced at once even if the former part could be possible. For instance, we're going to automate driving before we automate farming. Driving is just going from point A to point B. Farming will include driving (like tractors and whatnot) but also you need to watch the crops, check out what kind of pests/diseases you're dealing with, deal with and predict droughts, cold/hot days, etc. Simply put, we'll replace truck drivers that transport goods long before we'll replace farmers.

Now what does this mean? Well, truck drivers will be out of business but farmers wont. And the whole point of money and an economy is to ensure everyone gets what they need, but also contributes to the system as well. A doctor trades his work, time and expertise for the work, time and expertise of engineers, programmers, artists, business majors, etc when he buys something like a phone.

Now a system like this could work, if both the truck driver and the farmer were replaced by automation. Both people could still get food, and both people could contribute to society in other ways that may not necessarily require work. But all of this automation needs to come about at the same time, and be in sync. The automated farm won't work if the fertilizer plant, shipping, and all material mining/gathering isn't automated as well.

Money today is primarily an anonymous abstract metric of consumer demand, which we have the ability to measure by other, much better, means and project by quantitative analysis. Only about 8% of the money in the world exists as actual physical cash. The rest exists on the digital ledgers of banks. And this 8% is rapidly disappearing as we increasingly use electronic forms of money. So try to imagine what happens when all the money is digital and the details of all transactions are recorded. All just numbers on these digital bank ledgers representing digitally tracked transactions between one virtual place--one database entry--on the network of ledgers and another. We can analyze those numbers and devise algorithms that predict what happens to them pretty accurately. And if we can do that, we can automate exchange. We don't have to wait for people to do things to make the money flow from A to B on the network. We know, algorithmically, what they want and what they will most likely do and just do it in anticipation. We can do-away with the abstraction of currency and index the dynamic relative demand/value of everything to everything else. This is what futurists like Jacque Fresco call a 'resource based economy'. The relative demand/value of all natural resources and commodities deriving from them become the basis of all economic quantification. But for this to work we need the 'market' to be pretty transparent. Those algorithms need to develop a total digital awareness of the cost/value of things. And in the thousands of years since we invented money, this has been rather tricky. In the absence of coercion, profit is based on the divergence in the perception of value between the parties in an exchange. If Bob and Alice both know the true value of things they are trading, neither can profit. They can only barter equivalently. Profit is only possible for one if the other is ignorant. All profit is exploitation.

For centuries we've sought clever ways to alternately ferret-out or obfuscate the knowledge of costs to gain advantages over others on the market. In the past couple of centuries we've turned to advanced mathematics for this and, in the past century, applied computers. And the end result of this is that markets have become increasingly transparent and the prices of things around the world increasingly 'capitulated'--more-or-less the same all over the world. Only two commodities are now left that we, deliberately, haven't scientifically quantified; the cost of labor and the cost of money. And so most profit is rooted in the manipulation of those two things --which is why corporations and the finance industry have been waging war on wages for the past couple of generations. And here's where automation comes in. If you replace a human worker by automation, then your competitors know what the cost of that labor is in very concrete terms, because they can buy that same automation for the same price everywhere in the world. And that means the basis of profit comes down to the cost of money, and you get a race to the bottom in that cost as capital competes against itself until it too globally capitulates. If that happens, why then would anyone invest in anything? They would no longer be able to make a profit. Economics grinds to a halt. This is what is often referred to as the 'crisis of capitalism'.

The common mistake in discussions about the impact of automation is the assumption that labor and capital are separate. That while poor folks are replaced by machines, rich folk still reap the rewards of machine productivity because they own the machines. But workers and consumers are the same people and corporations don't actually own those machine --the banks and investors do. So, in fact, labor and capital are on different decks of the same sinking ship. This is why you actually have people in the finance world promoting UBI. It's capital's last best hope. The last way to keep the cash flowing through the economy. Capital is like a shark. If it isn't moving, it dies.

But once you've actually nailed down those last nebulous costs in the market system, have achieved total digital demand/value awareness, have obsolesced money by indexing the comparative value of everything to itself, you can algorithmically project demand as far into the future as you have computational capacity. And then you can let this projected demand drive the economy and let the market run on automatic. Total economic automation in parallel to total production automation. And what that means in a practical sense is that day-to-day production is justified simply by the algorithmic projection of people's common wants and needs, machines run to meet that demand, and everyone takes what they want off the store shelves for free-within-reason. This is how futurists arrive at the notion of a 'post-scarcity' situation and a money-less culture. If you have total digital demand/value awareness, money is redundant.

But if capital becomes obsolete, what initiates production? The capitalist system as it exists was premised on the necessity of large amounts of money to initiate industrialized production and created, with the fractional reserve banking system, for the purpose of extracting and collectivizing a portion of the productivity of society and putting it into the hands of a presumably specially skilled elite with the responsibility to use it to initialize production for the benefit of society. Profit is the reward for that. Capital is intended as a measure of merit. It's a bet by the people who wield it on the likely behavior and performance of the people who use it --who, no surprize, tend to belong to the same wealthy segment of society. But production technology is actually evolving toward the de-massification and dispersion of production. It is evolving toward merging with distribution and then immersion into the infrastructure of the built habitat like a municipal utility. The factory is already an anachronism. Most consumer goods in the world are produced in 'job shops' providing generic contract production. So futurists envision a new definition of capital as a digitally mediated social capital functioning as a better, direct, metric of merit. This means a new definition of wealth as dynamic social credit awarded as a direct result of the societal impact/importance of one's activity/intentions. The purpose of social credit is to empower individual and group activity through increased access to resources on the expectation of the value of that activity to society, rather than some assumption that people of a certain class are more deserving than others.

So that's how this automated post-scarcity, post-money, post-work utopia is supposed to work.
